structured_output.hypothesis: If Darwin's inference holds, the numeric age of the top of the Cretaceous (the end of the Chalk-depositing 'latter part of the Secondary period') on the international geological timescale is at least about 300 million years, so that the Weald denudation fits in the time since then.
structured_output.pass_criterion: The ICS chart gives an age of 300 Ma or more for the top of the Cretaceous (the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary), and an age of 270 Ma or more for the base of the Upper Cretaceous. Both must hold for the claim to be supported.
structured_output.fail_criterion: The ICS chart gives an age below 270 Ma for the top of the Cretaceous. The expected value is about 66 Ma, roughly 4.5 times less than Darwin's figure, which would refute the claim. Ages between 270 and 300 Ma count as inconclusive and not as a pass.
structured_output.interpretation: Darwin's 'latter part of the Secondary period' maps to the Late Cretaceous, the Chalk of the Weald's overlying cover. 'Years elapsed since' maps to the numeric age in Ma of the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary. This is the modern end of the Mesozoic, and the Chalk is the youngest Cretaceous strata of the Weald. The modern reinterpretation is that his 300 Myr is a duration computed from an assumed erosion rate of 1 inch per century, which was a physical assumption. We test the claim's conclusion, that more than 300 Myr have elapsed, against the radiometrically calibrated timescale. We do not test the erosion rate itself. The timescale fields used are the age of the base and top of the Cretaceous and of its Upper Cretaceous series, in Ma.

dataset.name: International Chronostratigraphic Chart
dataset.why_it_fits: The chart lists numeric boundary ages in Ma for every system, series and stage. These include the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary, at about 66.0 Ma, and the base of the Upper Cretaceous, at about 100.5 Ma. The chart is downloadable as PDF and image files, and the page also links machine-readable versions. Those ages can be compared directly with Darwin's 300 Myr.
